entities.name: Capetian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Capetian dynasty (987-1328 CE), founded when Hugh Capet was elected King of France in 987 CE and ruling France continuously for 341 years — the longest unbroken royal dynasty in European history — built the French state from a weak feudal monarchy controlling only the Île-de-France region around Paris into a centralized kingdom that dominated European politics. The Capetians' patient expansion — through inheritance, conquest, and marriage — gradually absorbed Normandy, Anjou, Poitiers, Languedoc, and other territories, creating the geographic and administrative basis of modern France.

Key Capetian reigns: Louis IX (Saint Louis, r. 1226-1270) — the most admired medieval French king, led two Crusades, reformed justice with the Parlement of Paris, banned trial by combat, and was canonized as a saint; Philip II Augustus (r. 1180-1223) quadrupled the crown's territory, drove the English out of Normandy (1204), and built Paris's first wall; Philip IV (r. 1285-1314) expelled the Jews (1306), destroyed the Knights Templar (1307-1314), and moved the papacy to Avignon (1309) — demonstrating the Capetians' transformation from feudal lord to Europe's most powerful monarch.

The Capetian legacy: the French administrative tradition (Parlement, royal council, tax system), the university of Paris (Sorbonne), French legal code, and the geographic consolidation of France. The dynasty ended when Charles IV died without male heirs in 1328, but Capetian cadet branches — Valois, Bourbon — continued ruling France until the French Revolution (1792) and beyond.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Capetian dynasty — ruling France unbroken for 341 years and building the French state from a small Île-de-France lordship to Europe's dominant kingdom — created the administrative and geographic foundations of France that persist to the present, making it one of history's most consequential state-building dynasties.
